papers.title: Autopoiesis: The organizational closure of social systems
papers.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The attempt to define living systems in terms of goal, purpose, function, etc. runs into serious conceptual difficulties. The theoretical biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela realized that any such attempt cannot capture what is distinctive about them: Their autonomy and unity. Goal, purpose, etc. always define the system in terms of something extrinsic, whereas living systems are unique because they maintain their unitary continuity of pattern despite the ceaseless turnover of their components. So, system‐closure is a prerequisite of their adequate conceptual comprehension. Maturana and Varela themselves found that system‐closure pertains exclusively to their organization, i.e. the set of relations among system‐components which unify them. For living systems this comprises the relation between the system‐components and the processes which they undergo. This relation is self‐referential because it is closed, i.e. it essentially (re)produces itself.</jats:p><jats:p>While this model worked very well in the biological domain, attempts to extend it to the social domain met with serious conceptual obstacles. The reason for this is that Maturana did not make a consistent enough application of it. He understood the components of social systems biologically (individuals, persons, etc.) and the relations between them socially (language). This inconsistency ruptured the system's organizational closure. Consequently organizational closure (autopoiesis) can be maintained only when both the components of social systems and their processes are of the same type: Social. This interpretation can be found in the work of Niklas Luhmann who recognizes that the components of social systems are not persons, individuals, actors or subjects but communicative actions themselves. This preserves the organizational closure of the system and permits the concept of autopoiesis to be used as a powerful instrument of social analysis.</jats:p>

papers.title: What Simulation Discloses: Emergence, Organizational Closure, and Autopoiesis in Self-Modifying Systems
papers.abstract:
<jats:p>This paper examines what simulation discloses about emergence, organizational closure, and autopoiesis in selfmodifying systems. Computational experiments in artificial life can do philosophical work by making explicit and testable the organizational assumptions built into these concepts. We use the Compositional Disclosure Model (CDM), a self-modifying computational system with a second-order cybernetic structure, in which the organization acts on its own operative repertoire, as a bounded conceptual case study. The system discovers macro-actions through compositional graph reasoning and verifies organizational closure through modal temporal logic. The experimentâ€™s philosophical contribution lies in the question it makes tractable: when an agent discovers a forward-right diagonal action by composing forward and right movement primitives, has it discovered something genuinely new, or merely disclosed what was always latent in the relational structure of its base schema? We argue that emergence in simulation is characteristically a matter of disclosure rather than creation, a shift from latent relational structure to manifest organizational form. We further argue that disclosure is a semiotic event: a latent relation becomes operative under an interpretive criterion and, once admitted, revises the horizon of subsequent action. Formal verification functions here not as proof of life but as epistemic scaffolding, making organizational assumptions explicit, comparable, and revisable. Across repeated runs, the disclosed action structure yields stable organizational consequences. The central claim is therefore methodological as much as metaphysical: computational experiments of this kind can transform disputes about emergence and organization into disciplined, revisable objects of inquiry.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Data/Code available at: https://github.com/Ohara124c41/computational-disclosure-models</jats:p>

papers.title: Operationalizing autopoiesis beyond organisms via repair-closure
papers.abstract: <jats:p>We propose a perturbation-testable criterion for organizational autonomy beyond organisms: \emph{repair-closure}, the ability of a system to restore the constraints that constitute its organization after targeted perturbations within a bounded horizon.We develop a proof-complete framework in which viability is a local-to-global consistency problem and viable regimes are global sections of a viability subsheaf (a structure enforcing local-to-global consistency) over a finite compartment complex.To ground the theory biologically, we provide a worked ecosystem-module example inspired by the sulfidic chemoautotrophic Movile Cave system, specifying candidate constraints, concrete perturbation protocols, measurable readouts, and plausible repair pathways.We distinguish geological boundaries from internally maintained \emph{functional boundaries} and prove that repair-closure implies invariant maintenance of such boundaries under perturbation.We formalize openness via explicit interfaces and prove persistence of coupled viability under slack witnesses.Finally, we give an implementable computational pipeline and quantitative Lipschitz--slack radii that turn robustness claims into explicit parameter neighborhoods.</jats:p>

papers.title: Closure Without Enclosure: Fungal Mycelia and the Distributed Form of Autopoiesis
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Autopoietic organization persists by producing and repairing the components and boundary conditions that realize the network of production itself. Filamentous fungi provide a stringent distributed case: a mycelium grows through moving apical production fronts, continuously remodels its wall, externalizes part of digestion into the surrounding substrate, reallocates resources through a changing network, regulates cytoplasmic continuity through septa, fuses only under recognition constraints, and may maintain multinuclear or heterokaryotic organization. The formalization retains viability localization, monadic production/repair, boundary production, admissibility, and viable global regimes as the defining autopoietic semantics. Fungal transport, wall, regulatory, nuclear, and fusion layers are coupled by limits and internal relations; when layerwise production/repair realizations are available, their coupling is formed in the Eilenberg–Moore category so that the composite inherits a canonical realization without assuming linear state spaces. Local-to-global viability is governed by sheaf descent. Environmental substrate transformation is represented in a slice topos, separating produced fungal interfaces from extracellular transformation while preserving relative autopoietic closure. Growth, fusion, injury, and repair are represented by correspondences between changing mycelial bases and internal viability relations; viable identity is existence of a section of the resulting history object, not persistence of fixed anatomy. Septal plugging changes descent conditions, anastomosis requires recognition-admissible effective descent, and mycorrhizal exchange is a pullback coupling between distinct closures. This architecture yields discriminating empirical tests: organization-aware interface measurements should predict survival, fusion, and symbiotic persistence beyond morphology alone; matched morphologies may have different viable outcomes; and reducing connectivity can restore viable continuation after local damage. Filamentous fungi therefore instantiate closure without enclosure and expose biological individuality as continuity of viability-localized self-production across changing boundaries.</jats:p>

papers.title: Business Autopoiesis Through Process Referencing
papers.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, the concept of autopoietic system is assumed to stem from the theory of social communication systems, which reproduce all their specific structures and self-referential processes. This chapter aims at the analysis of business process development and management. The main goal is to present an original framework of business process management. Through this framework, business processes can be interpreted as autonomic artifacts which are created, discovered, explored, and disseminated within social communities of practice. This constant reproduction of processes and their dissemination allows the social organization to exist, cope with internal complexity, and achieve its operational goals. The chapter consists of three main parts. The first part covers the systematic literature review on business process mining and referencing. The second part includes the discussion on presented business process framework. The last part comprises a case study to present and discuss the application of the framework for the development of academic virtual education processes.</jats:p>

papers.title: Viruses as Living Systems? Borrowed Closure and the Limits of Autopoiesis
papers.abstract: <jats:p>In 2022, Yolles and Frieden argued that viruses are alive by moving the criterion for life from metabolism to organisation, arguing the genome–capsid couple to be autopoietic. This study reframes that conclusion with two constructs of Fisher-Generative Informational Realism (FGIR): the CAS/CAAS boundary, separating a Complex Adaptive System (CAS), adaptive but not self-sustaining, from a self-sustaining Complex Adaptive Autopoietic System (CAAS); and the coercivity law, which requires a system’s protoenergy, the informational effort of holding a configuration in persistent form, to exceed a threshold. The verdict “viruses are not autopoietic” conflates two conditions. Viruses satisfy the topological condition, the couple being a genuine self-producing network, but fail the resourcing condition, since the capacity to maintain it belongs to the host: “borrowed closure”, which we derive formally. Identifying the viral protoenergy with the draw on the host, and letting self-supply return only when the lineage’s translation machinery is complete, yields a host-budget equation with a saddle-node bifurcation at a critical completion fraction. Given a near-all-or-nothing return of self-supply, the barrier is structural rather than statistical, and it survives stochastic, epidemiological and delayed reformulations; its value is illustrative. The account is falsifiable and taxonomically agnostic, as the ribosome-encoding but host-dependent bacterium Carsonella ruddii shows, and crossings into self-sufficiency are observed only downward.</jats:p>

papers.title: Viability-Localized Autopoiesis II: An Operator Calculus for Probes, Contexts, Scale Translation, and Empirical Closure Tests
papers.abstract: <jats:p>A preceding BioSystems article formulated autopoiesis as viability-localized self-production: biological closure is evaluated after viability localization, production and repair are represented by a generative realization structure, boundary maintenance is made explicit, admissible boundary states constrain production, and at least one viable global regime must exist. The present article develops the second stage of that framework. It does not redefine autopoiesis. It develops an operator layer for analyzing how a specified autopoietic datum is probed, compared across contexts, transported across scales, extended from partial data, and tested against empirical constraints.The paper introduces an autopoietic operator system composed of a viability-localized autopoietic core together with probe families, context fibrations, descent data, scale-translation operators, data-extension operators, and diagnostic signatures. The main result is an operator-insufficiency theorem: fixed points, monads, sheaves, admissibility predicates, internal languages, context fibrations, adjunctions, Kan extensions, and Yoneda profiles are individually insufficient to analyze viability-localized autopoiesis, because each misses at least one relevant failure mode. These include production failure, boundary-admissibility failure, local-to-global gluing failure, context dependence, scale-translation distortion, and probe-relative indistinguishability.The operator calculus is anchored in standard biological data structures and workflows: flux balance analysis in the BiGG E. coli core model, epithelial cyst and lumen assays, viral host-factor dependence, planarian perturbation-response profiles, ecological feasibility networks, metabolic model reduction and reconstruction, and single-cell reference mapping. A reproducible flux-balance calculation shows that aerobic glucose, anaerobic glucose, and pyruvate-dehydrogenase-blocked conditions all admit viable global flux sections in the E. coli core model, but with distinct biomass objectives and context defects. The result is an operational continuation of viability-localized autopoiesis: the first stage specifies what counts as autopoietic closure, and the present paper specifies how such closure is interrogated by probes, contexts, scale changes, and empirical data.</jats:p>

papers.title: Formalizing autopoiesis: Toward a Categorical-Thermodynamic Calculus of Closure
Tipping the Balance: Autopoiesis and Governance
papers.abstract: A modern society, according to autopoietic and other analyses, comprises social systems that show organizational closure and selfrreferentiality, partly explaining widely perceived regulatory failure. This article compares four possible mechanisms for governance or steering of such systems, compatible with their autopoiesis: the use of subsidy, partnership with intermediary bodies, reflexive law, and a technique of government intervention that is ancient and common but not recognized, here named collibration. Some social actors exist mainly to check and balance other actors (e.g., employers' organizations and trade unions, or buyers and sellers in a market) and are self-referential only as a pair system This pair system is then self-policing but can be steered, within limits, by tipping the balance that is being maintained-as exemplified by price-loading taxes, cooling-off periods, and sport handicapping.

papers.title: Rewriting Theory: From Autopoiesis to Communication
papers.abstract: This paper analyzes the causes and motives for the transition to a communication‐based theory of social systems in the late work of Niklas Luhmann. In the first part of this paper, I present a brief sketch of advances in the field of cybernetics and systems research. I give special attention to some basic concepts introduced by Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela: autopoiesis, organizational closure and enaction. In the second part, I discuss how these ideas may contribute to a ‘conceptual revolution’ in the social and behavioral sciences. In the late work of Niklas Luhmann, attempts to incorporate the idea of autopoiesis in his own social theory resulted in the preference for a communication‐based, instead of an action‐based, theory of social systems. Moreover, given the current transition to the information age or the knowledge society, it can also be argued that structural changes in society nowadays favor the rise of a communication‐based theory of social systems. Copyright © 2012 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

papers.title: Autopoiesis, Autonomy, and Organizational Biology: Critical Remarks on “Life After Ashby”
papers.abstract: In this paper we criticize the "Ashbyan interpretation" of autopoietic theory by showing that Ashby's framework and the autopoietic one are based on distinct, often incompatible, assumptions and they aim at addressing different issues. We also suggest that in order to better understand autopoiesis and its implications, a different and wider set of theoretical contributions, developed previously or at the time autopoiesis was formulated, needs to be taken into consideration: among the others, the works of Rosen, Weiss and Piaget. By analyzing the concepts of organization and closure, the idea of components and the role of materiality in the theory proposed by Maturana and Varela, we advocate the view that autopoiesis necessarily entails self-production and intrinsic instability and that can be realized only in domains characterized by the same transformative and processual properties exhibited by the molecular domain. From this theoretical standpoint it can be demonstrated that autopoietic theory does neither commit to a sharp dualism between organization and structure nor to a reflexive view of downward causation, thus avoiding the respective strong criticisms.
papers.categories: Autopoiesis; Autonomy; Cognitive science; Sociology; Psychology

papers.title: You Have Mail: Set-Theoretic Types for Actors
papers.authors: Giuseppe Castagna; Luca Padovani; Daniele Varacca; Amine Nasri
papers.abstract:
We present a type system for the processes of Elixir, a dynamic language based on the actor model whose static type system covers only its functional core. Each process is typed by $\mathtt{pid}(t)$, where the ``interface'' $t$ is the type of the messages the process expects in its mailbox: sends are checked against the recipient's interface, and receives rely on the interface of the process that performs them.
  One of the difficulties of typing Elixir is that mailboxes are implicit: a function shipped in a message may evaluate $\mathtt{self()}$ and execute receive instructions, and both refer to whichever process eventually runs the function---$\mathtt{self()}$ returns that process's pid, receive reads that process's mailbox---so the mailbox they act on is not known where the function is written. We solve this problem by inferring, for every function, bounds on the type of the mailboxes it can be used with; as a result, the system types higher-order functions that travel in messages even when they contain reference to $\mathtt{self()}$ and receive instructions.
  The only new annotation the programmer writes is the interface of each spawned process; everything else is inferred by reusing the existing subtyping and constraint-resolution machinery of Elixir, and the system is proved sound.
  For legacy code, the interface can be reconstructed from the receive clauses: what the branches do with their messages bounds it from above, and the most permissive solution is sharp enough to recover received pids and closures.

papers.title: Local Clustering Tests and Botnet Localization in Sparse Random Geometric Networks
papers.authors: Luca Di Persio; Gianmarco Bet; Youness Outaleb
papers.abstract: We use local clustering to test for botnets in sparse random geometric networks. Under the null hypothesis, the vertices are independent uniform points on a fixed-dimensional torus, with edges determined by a distance threshold. Under the alternative, an unknown set of vertices ignores the geometry and connects independently with the same marginal edge probability. Every prescribed vertex has the same marginal binomial degree law under both hypotheses, so its degree alone carries no information. Triangle closure, however, distinguishes the two models. Under the null, conditional on a degree of at least two, the local clustering coefficient has exact mean $C_d>0$, a known constant that depends only on the dimension. Under the alternative, the corresponding mean is $p_n$ for a bot. For a non-bot, the corresponding mixture mean converges to $C_d$ when the botnet size is $o(n)$. We prove non-asymptotic concentration bounds, an exponential bound on the worst-case risk of a scan test, and exact-support recovery. For every deterministic sequence $1\leq k_n=o(n)$, if $μ_n=(n-1)p_n$ satisfies $μ_n/\log n\to\infty$, the local rule recovers the botnet with probability tending to one, uniformly over all label sets of size $k_n$. The proof combines geometric U-statistics, bounded differences on random neighborhoods, and a stability bound showing that genuine vertices retain their geometric clustering when bots form only a vanishing fraction of their neighbors. The test does not use the latent positions. The theorem assumes that the model parameters are known, although $C_d$ can instead be estimated consistently. In the high-expected-degree regime, the rule also works for a single bot.

papers.title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
papers.authors: Weile Li; Yunfan Lou; Muqing Shi; Zihao Zhang; Zhenbiao Huang; Boxian Yao; Xiyu Zhu; Zhibo Pang
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.

papers.title: When Suspicion Adds Up: A Stochastic Framework for Optimizing Honeypot-Based Insider-Threat Detection
papers.authors: Saharnaz Mehrani; Lujia Zhan; Mohsen Emadikhiav; Payman Dehghanian
papers.abstract: Insider threats pose security risks when employees or other trusted users misuse their access to organizational systems. Detecting these threats is difficult because harmful activity can resemble routine behavior. Honeypots, or decoy resources monitored for suspicious interactions, can provide evidence of potentially malicious activity. We develop a decision framework that models evidence accumulation through honeypot interactions using a continuous-time Markov chain and jointly selects honeypot counts and monitoring horizons to minimize expected losses from malicious activity and false detections. For thresholds of two and three interactions, we derive closed-form true- and false-detection probabilities and expected detection times conditional on detection within the monitoring horizon. We characterize boundary cases and establish stochastic-ordering results. Our numerical results highlight the value of the proposed framework across different settings.

papers.title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
papers.authors: Francesco Belardinelli; Flavio Corradini; Matteo Leonesi
papers.abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

papers.title: FirstCross: Convex Single-Photon 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views
papers.authors: Chi-Wei Lee; Cheng-Han Chiang; Yi-Chun Chang; An-Kai Chen; Po-Chih Kuo
papers.abstract: Single-photon lidar records the arrival time of each returning photon, enabling 3D reconstruction from few views and scarce photons. However, leading neural methods such as Transientangelo require over an hour of non-convex per-scene optimization, and their accuracy degrades as photon flux decreases. We propose FirstCross, a network-free approach that instead solves a short sequence of convex problems on a voxel grid. For a solid object, the Poisson likelihood of a ray with given signal and background rates depends on the scene solely through its first crossing, the point where the ray first enters the object. Decomposing this likelihood yields two tractable terms. The first penalizes surfaces in front of detected photons and admits a tight convex closure, namely volume rendering with a running-maximum transmittance in place of NeRF's product transmittance. The second accounts for photons that no surface explains and admits a convex upper bound once the object is assumed to be thick behind each detected surface point. Compared with Transientangelo under its own real-data protocol, FirstCross achieves lower depth error across every test scene, view count, and flux level. With three views and 100 times fewer photons than at the protocol's lowest flux, our mean object depth error stays under half of Transientangelo's with all photons. Given our detected surface points, the best classical fusion has 1.3 to 1.8 times our three-view error across flux levels. On real room-scale captures with 1% of their photons, TransientNeRF has 2.8 to 7.7 times our error. FirstCross lets few-view single-photon scanners cut exposure to 1% and reconstruct an object in about a minute on one GPU.

papers.title: A Surrogate Detector Model for the MINERvA Open Dataset
papers.authors: Sparshita Dey; Alexander Himmel; David Last; Liang Liu; Pedro Machado; Vishvas Pandey; Linyan Wan
papers.abstract: The growing availability of open neutrino data promises broader scrutiny of interaction models, but a critical barrier remains: mapping theoretical predictions into reconstructed observables, which previously required computationally intensive methods inaccessible outside the original experimental collaborations. In this work, we present a probabilistic surrogate of the MINERvA detector response, trained on an open simulation dataset to map generator-level final-state particles and interaction geometry to reconstructed observables, without relying on generator-specific interaction labels. We assess its fidelity through conditional response distributions, reconstructed observables, and classifier-based closure tests. We further demonstrate generalization beyond the limitations of conventional phase-space-dependent reweighting by withholding two-particle-two-hole interactions entirely from training and showing that the surrogate reproduces their reconstructed response within the estimated uncertainties. In an end-to-end application to MINERvA charged-current inclusive muon-neutrino data, we reproduce selection efficiencies and purities and forward-fold predictions from GENIE, NuWro, and GiBUU for direct comparison with measurements. By moving theoretical predictions into reconstructed space rather than unfolding the data, this work establishes a reusable interface between neutrino interaction models and experimental observations, expanding the scope of physics accessible through open datasets.

papers.title: Uninorm constructions on bounded trellises via closure and interior operators
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which six closure- or interior-based operations on bounded trellises are uninorms. These operations incorporate triangular norms, triangular conorms, or both, and form three order-dual pairs. Since the underlying pseudo-order need not be transitive and meet and join need not be associative, standard lattice arguments do not apply directly. Under a fixed ambient transitivity assumption, the first pair is characterized by image, monotonicity, and compatibility conditions for the associated maps on elements incomparable with the neutral element; an additional comparison condition used in earlier sufficient constructions is shown to be redundant. Complete characterizations are also obtained for the variants with an absorbing endpoint, including both nondegenerate and degenerate interval cases. For the pair involving both a triangular norm and a triangular conorm, we derive exact comparison conditions requiring the triangular norm to take the value~$0$, or dually the triangular conorm to take the value~$1$, in the relevant cases. These conditions reduce to the usual incomparability assumptions in the absence of nontrivial zero- or one-divisors. On bounded lattices, the closure and interior conditions simplify to explicit identities or image restrictions. Finite proper-trellis examples clarify the role and limitations of the ambient transitivity assumptions.

papers.title: F.W.J. Schelling and autopoiesis.
papers.authors: Vrabec M; Jureček M; Švorcová J
papers.abstract: This paper explores certain conceptual resonances between Friedrich W. J. Schelling's philosophy of nature and a biological theory of autopoiesis developed by Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, and its subsequent extensions. While these frameworks emerged from different historical and intellectual traditions, they both challenge a mechanistic and reductionist understanding of life by emphasising self-organisation, the maintenance of boundaries, and relational autonomy. Schelling's dynamic monism describes nature as a self-productive process within which living beings arise through internal purposiveness, self-regulation, and resistance to external forces. Along similar lines, autopoiesis defines living systems as autonomous and self-producing networks which maintain their identity through structural coupling with the environment. Drawing on key notions such as cyclicity, reciprocal causality, embodied cognition, and self-representation, we argue that Schelling's philosophical approach towards the living can be viewed as analogical to many insights coming from the autopoietic theory.

papers.title: A Tale of Two Principles-Towards a Relational Perspective on the Free Energy Principle.
papers.abstract: The Free Energy Principle (FEP) offers a physically grounded account of intentional properties in mind and life, framed in the context of Dynamical Systems Theory. Because of this generality, it was proposed as a formal basis to formalize the study of biological autonomy, autopoiesis, and enactive cognition. Yet, those approaches are centered by definition on describing how biological and cognitive agents are "laying down a path in walking", or (re)constructing their own biological/cognitive structure through engagement with the world. Drawing from Rosen's relational biology, we argue that such processes are by construction outside a "Newtonian" description in terms of well-defined observables and their dynamics. Rather, we draw from the thermodynamics of observation and biological computation to demonstrate the emergence of contextuality: the participatory production of observables against which the agent regulates their activity. We suggest a complementarity between Friston's classical FEP and Fields' relational FEP, describing, respectively, the dynamics within a biological/cognitive space and the construction of that space. Finally, we propose a structural realist understanding of this complementarity where both principles act on a physically embedded system of biological constraints, rather than an abstract mathematical space assumed to fully represent biological/cognitive organization.

papers.title: The computational genesis of a self: Representational time and self-modeling in living systems.
papers.abstract: The transition from inanimate physicochemical dynamics to autonomous agency represents a fundamental challenge across theoretical biology and cognitive science. While traditional accounts have approached this transition through descriptive frameworks of autopoiesis, anticipatory systems, or the free energy principle, a formal deductive derivation linking computational irreducibility to functional agency has remained elusive. Here, a deductive framework demonstrates that core attributes of biological agency, specifically representational time, forward predictive processing, and self-modeling, emerge as operational necessities for an autonomous agent persisting within a computationally irreducible environment under a defined operational regime of delayed hazards and counterfactual pre-commitment. Grounded in organizational closure and viability theory, this framework establishes three principal deductive results. First, it is demonstrated that purely reactive behavioral strategies fail under observationally aliased environmental states requiring mutually incompatible viability-preserving actions; persisting under delayed viability hazards without lethal trial-and-error mandates the internal synthesis of a tripartite representational time. Second, this representational time is shown to share the operational organization of counterfactual forward prediction. Third, drawing upon closed-loop regulator theory, the Conant-Ashby theorem, and the internal model principle, it is established that evaluating candidate interventions over extended horizons (H > 1) in a coupled system requires internalizing the agent's own generative action dynamics, yielding a functional self-model distinct from simple state-dependent regulation. These formal derivations are subsequently grounded in concrete molecular and cellular phenomena, including cyanobacterial KaiABC timekeeping, synthetic protocellular clocks, microbial adaptive regulation, and bacterial chemotaxis, explicitly demarcating experimentally demonstrated substrates from theoretical extrapolations. Finally, the framework develops a theoretical bridge connecting computational irreducibility to the semiotic hypothesis of organic codes as physical adaptors bridging decoupled biological domains, incorporating the code-mediator-artifact distinction. The analysis concludes that within the specified operational regime, functional self-representation emerges as an inevitable computational consequence of autonomous persistence.

papers.title: Genealogies of organizational closure: from logical paradox to mind in life.
papers.authors: Rubin S; Roli A; Stano P; Damiano L
papers.abstract: Organizational closure occupies a central position in contemporary theories of autonomy, anticipation, agency, sense making, and the continuity between life and mind. Its investigation has given rise to a diverse landscape of related explanations, including closure to information, cyclic closure, operational closure, semantic closure, closure-to-efficient causation, metabolic closure, and closure of constraints. Although each of these explanatory approaches captures important aspects of organizational closure, their proliferation has often generated conceptual ambiguity. As a result, organizational closure is frequently conflated with feedback loops, recursive algorithms, self-organization, or biochemical cycles. This paper develops a genealogical conceptual analysis of the research programs from which these various accounts emerged, tracing their origins across mathematical logic, first- and second-order cybernetics, general systems theory, thermodynamics, metabolic theory, relational biology, and the biology of cognition. In doing so, it provides a principled framework for assessing the commitments involved whenever a notion of closure is invoked, while clarifying the origins of these explanations and the relations among them. Particular attention is devoted to the roles of self-reference, circular causality, replication maps, semantics, free energy, automata, operations, and constraints in shaping the current understanding of organizational closure. On this basis, the study advances the interpretative thesis that organizational closure is most coherently understood as a circular organization of efficient causes through which living beings continuously produce and maintain the conditions of their own existence. From this perspective, organizational closure appears irreducible to purely algorithmic descriptions inherited from the Church-Turing thesis-not because living beings cannot be simulated in specific respects, but because the causal production of the conditions of their own realization cannot be exhaustively characterized as a state-determined syntactic procedure. This interpretation helps clarify the distinctions between organizational closure and the notions with which it is often conflated, while providing a framework for assessing current debates concerning artificial intelligence, large language models (LLMs), semantic meaning, and sense making in the face of ambiguity and logical paradox.

papers.title: Experimental probes of autopoietic self-maintenance.
papers.abstract: Autopoietic closure is a constitutive causal property of a living system: a recursively organized network produces the components and boundary conditions that regenerate that same network. Experiments can reveal, discriminate, or fail to detect this organization, but they do not create or define it. This article develops a categorical account of the relation between autopoietic organization and its experimental representation. Building on a topos-theoretic formulation of viability-localized self-production, the paper distinguishes three levels: the natural biological system, a formal organizational surrogate, and the observer-side profile generated by experimental protocols. A category of organizational models and a category of typed protocols are defined explicitly, together with a realization functor from protocols to formal test objects. The Yoneda lemma then characterizes formal models through all formal tests, while restriction to an experimentally available protocol family yields a partial response profile. Equivalence of restricted profiles establishes organizational equivalence only when that protocol family is conservative on a specified class of candidate models. This condition converts the idea of an adequate assay panel into a precise, model-relative criterion without conflating experimental accessibility with operational closure. The framework also distinguishes diagnostic from predictive uses, accommodates destructive assays, differentiation, environmental context, and one-off experimental histories, and limits its claim about emergence to local-to-global compatibility. A worked reaction-network example shows how perturbation profiles discriminate highly resilient from fragile self-maintaining organizations while the causal closure remains defined by the reaction network itself. The result is an experiment-oriented semantics for testing formal models of autopoietic self-maintenance, not an observational redefinition of autopoiesis.

papers.title: Aging as cross-hallmark obstruction amplification: A sheaf-theoretic model of repair closure, senescence, inflammation, and regenerative failure.
papers.abstract: The twelve hallmarks of aging describe heterogeneous molecular, cellular, tissue, and systemic changes but do not by themselves explain how they become an organism-level loss of repair capacity. Aging is represented as a cost-constrained, stochastic loss of autopoietic repair closure. Hallmark processes are organized as coupled local-to-global constraint layers on a finite biological complex: global sections represent compatible repair modes, while a connecting morphism measures when coherent regulatory states generate material-repair incompatibilities. The principal accounting identity states that coupled repair reserve equals material-repair closure plus regulatory-interface closure minus cross-hallmark obstruction rank. The identity follows from standard exact-sequence and rank-nullity arguments; its biological content lies in the construction of the coupled aging object and the interpretation of obstruction rank as cross-hallmark repair incompatibility. A dynamical extension places repair under finite, fallible control, stochastic perturbation, delayed feedforward dependence, and an explicit viability domain, allowing additional surveillance to reduce global repair when coupling costs exceed local gains. A reproducible two-compartment example specifies stalk variables, restriction maps, coboundary matrices, H0, H1, connecting-map rank, and an approximate persistence interval. Published epigenetic-clock, skeletal-muscle regeneration, and senolytic results are literature-anchored mappings rather than empirical validation. The proposed invariants therefore target one structural dimension of aging: loss of achievable, globally compatible repair under finite biological control.

papers.title: Organizational closure through regenerative signaling as a possible basis for conscious awareness.
papers.abstract: Along the lines of neuronal global workspace theories, the paper hypothesizes that active neural signal regeneration in recurrent, re-entrant circuits could constitute an organizational basis for states of conscious awareness. In this view, brains are self-production systems that regenerate their own informational, signal states ("neural autopoiesis"). States of awareness themselves depend critically on sustained regeneration of sets of neural signals in local and global circuits. The set of regenerated signals at each moment determines the specific contents of consciousness. Two hypotheses are proposed. H1: Organizational closure and with it, awareness, is achieved when regenerative, self-production loops are completed, such that a stable set of signal productions is sustained. The organization of informational processes stabilizes and closes on itself. H2: Neural coding is critical for signal regeneration. Neural signals must be properly encoded in order for them to be regenerated and thereby affect the contents of awareness. In addition to simple signal suppressions at their points of origin, one means by which general anesthetic agents may abolish awareness is by scrambling neural signals. Rendering internal control signals incoherent by altering within- and across-neuron rate profiles and/or temporal patternings may disrupt signal regeneration in local and global circuits. The two hypotheses are agnostic with respect to neural coding. Our own signal-centric time-domain (TD) brain theory framework is presented to illustrate how signal regeneration could be mediated by local and global temporal codes and neural temporal processing networks. Similarities and differences between TD, global neuronal workspaces (GNW), recurrent processing (RP), integrated information (IIT) and predictive processing (PP) are discussed. Empirical testing will necessitate solving the neural coding problem at multiple system levels. This will involve investigating correlations and causal linkages between regeneration of tracked neural signals and states of awareness as well as between alternative candidate neural codes and the contents of awareness. Rhythm-tagged stimuli and high temporal resolution neural recordings are proposed to enable tracking of specific neural signals throughout the brain under conditions of waking vs. sleep vs. anesthesia, with masking and unmasking signal/noise levels. Some philosophical comments regarding organization as a potential basis for consciousness are made.
